ASTM has a non-drop-in jet fuel group to explore alternative chemistries. Currently, there is no ASTM standard for non-drop-in synthetic aviation fuels. There are substantial barriers to non- drop-in liquid aviation fuels that are not compatible with existing aircraft and fuel infrastructure. Extensive, long-term research on materials, aircraft, and infrastructure equipment would be needed to demonstrate compatibility and enable market acceptance. Another critical safety aspect is segregating Jet A/SAF at an airport from an alternate liquid aviation fuel to avoid contamination. Other barriers include potential resistance to microbial contamination, electrical capacitance differences, and impacts on fuel level readings (Dasgupta et al. 2023). While flow rates would likely be the same as Jet A, emergency procedures could vary based on the properties of these fuels. Handling and use guides would need to be developed to ensure safe practices. Some of the Jet X-type fuels under consideration would not have aromatics. Aromatics lead to soot formation, which contributes to contrail formation. There are challenges for fuels without aromatics due to impacts on elastomer seals such as O-rings in engines. Using replacement aromatics could mitigate materials impacts. Potential pathways to produce biogenic aromatics include upgrading biofuels via catalytic fast pyrolysis or Diels-Alder cycloaddition reactions (Weglin and Meier 2024). The Federal Aviation Administration’s Center for Excellence for Alternative Jet Fuels and Environment Project 66 is evaluating if fuels with high thermal stability could improve fuel burn in engines and performance (Federal Aviation Administration 2025). The Transportation Research Board proposed a project, which has not been conducted, to evaluate barriers to integrating Jet X into airport infrastructure and develop a guidebook for airports to assist with future fuel infrastructure (Murphy 2024). This project would also perform a case study to assess economic and environmental impacts of integrating Jet X into airport tank farms. Another proposed activity is developing a roadmap with a timeline for commercialization, solutions to address infrastructure challenges, and actions stakeholders need to take to enable Jet X. As Jet X fuels are non-drop-in liquid hydrocarbon synthetic fuels under investigation, little is known about their future properties and the associated impacts on infrastructure. The information on Jet X is limited due to its early stage of development.
